```{r setup, include=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)
```


#Tutorial 1: From point estimates to intervals
##1.1 Fitting a simple model
We’ll use the built-in mtcars dataset for simplicity (swap for a dataset relevant to you if prefer).

```{r}
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + cyl, data = mtcars)
coefs <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
coefs
```

##1.2 Forest plot of coefficients

```{r}
A<-coefs |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  labs(title = "Coefficient estimates with 95% CI",
       x = "Estimate", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

A
```


##1.3 The “dynamite plot” version
Exercise 1.1 - Reproduce the same information as a bar chart with error bars (geom_col + geom_errorbar), using estimate for bar height and conf.low/conf.high for the error bars. Place this next to your forest plot (e.g. with patchwork).

Write 2-3 sentences: which is clearer for negative coefficients? What does the bar chart visually imply about zero that the forest plot doesn’t?

```{r}
B<-coefs %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=estimate, x = term)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = term, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  theme_minimal()

A | B
```
forest plot is better. 
bar chart shows zero at the top and negatives falling down below zero, which is not visually shown in the forest plot. 


##1.4 Labelling intervals correctly
Exercise 1.2 - Refit the model and extract both a 90% and a 99% CI (conf.level argument to tidy() or confint()). Plot both intervals for each coefficient on the same forest plot (e.g. thin line for 99%, thick line for 90%, point for the estimate). Make sure your legend/ caption makes it unambiguous which interval is which. This is the single most common omission in uncertainty plots.

```{r}
library(purrr)
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + cyl, data = mtcars)
lvls <- c(0.9, 0.99)

coefs <- map_dfr(lvls, 
                 ~ cbind(tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = .x),
                         level = .x)) %>%
  mutate(level = as.factor(level))
  
coefs
#35 is 0.9
```


```{r}
coefs |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  select(term, level, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term, group=level)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high,  linewidth = level),
                 ) +
  labs(title = "Coefficient estimates with 90 and 99% CI",
       x = "Estimate", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
    scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c("0.9" = 2, "0.99" = 0.8), # Define specific thicknesses
    name = "Confidence Level")
```

#Tutorial 2: Prediction intervals and ribbons
##2.1 Fitted line with confidence ribbon

```{r}
fit2 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

newdata <- data.frame(wt = seq(min(mtcars$wt), max(mtcars$wt), length.out = 100))

ci <- predict(fit2, newdata = newdata, interval = "confidence")
pi <- predict(fit2, newdata = newdata, interval = "prediction")

plot_df <- newdata |>
  mutate(
    fit = ci[, "fit"],
    ci_lwr = ci[, "lwr"], ci_upr = ci[, "upr"],
    pi_lwr = pi[, "lwr"], pi_upr = pi[, "upr"]
  )

ggplot(plot_df, aes(wt)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lwr, ymax = ci_upr), alpha = 0.4, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit)) +
  geom_point(data = mtcars, aes(wt, mpg), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Confidence interval ribbon",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "MPG") +
  theme_minimal()
```


##2.2 Adding the prediction interval
Exercise 2.1 - Add the prediction interval as a second ribbon (different fill/alpha) underneath the confidence ribbon. Make sure the legend or caption clearly distinguishes the two. You can refer back to this week’s lecture 1 distinction on CI-vs-PI.

```{r}
ggplot(plot_df, aes(wt)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi_lwr, ymax = pi_upr), alpha = 0.2, fill = "orange") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lwr, ymax = ci_upr), alpha = 0.6, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit)) +
  geom_point(data = mtcars, aes(wt, mpg), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Confidence interval ribbon",
       subtitle = "confidence interval in blue, prediction interval in orange",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "MPG") +
  theme_minimal()
```


Exercise 2.2 - Compare this ribbon plot to a Week 5 ensemble ribbon plot (your random walk summary). Both use geom_ribbon with similar code. In 2-3 sentences: what is the source of the band’s width in each case? Could a reader tell the difference just by looking at the plot, without reading axis labels/captions? What does that imply about captioning?

week five's ribbons take the intervals as quantile of the random walks. The proportions of the walks in that range, 90% of data are within this range. This ribbon takes the confidence interval (likely area where an unknown population parameter point would fall, e.g. mean) and the prediction intervals (where a new point would likely fall within). Not the same. Not easy to know unless read explicitly told. 

##2.3 Multiple predictors
Exercise 2.3 - Using fit from Tutorial (part) 1 (above; multiple predictors), produce a ribbon plot of predicted mpg vs wt, holding hp and cyl at their mean values. Note in your caption that this is a conditional prediction.

Discuss briefly why holding other variables at their means is a simplification.

```{r}
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + cyl, data = mtcars)

x <- seq(min(mtcars$wt), max(mtcars$wt), length.out = 100)

# Create newdata with hp and cyl held at their means
newdata <- data.frame(
  wt = x,
  hp = mean(mtcars$hp),
  cyl = mean(mtcars$cyl)
)

pred_ci <- predict(fit, newdata = newdata, interval = "confidence")
pred_pi <- predict(fit, newdata = newdata, interval = "prediction")

plot_df <- data.frame(
  wt = x,
  fit = pred_ci[, "fit"],
  ci_lwr = pred_ci[, "lwr"], ci_upr = pred_ci[, "upr"],
  pi_lwr = pred_pi[, "lwr"], pi_upr = pred_pi[, "upr"])
  
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x=wt, y = fit)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi_lwr, ymax = pi_upr), alpha = 0.2, fill = "orange") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lwr, ymax = ci_upr), alpha = 0.6, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit)) +
  geom_point(data = mtcars, aes(wt, mpg), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Confidence interval ribbon, hp and cyl held at their means",
       subtitle = "confidence interval in blue, prediction interval in orange",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "MPG") +
  theme_minimal()

```

#Tutorial 3: Distributional uncertainty

##Bootstrap refresher

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n_boot <- 1000

boot_coefs <- replicate(n_boot, {
  boot_sample <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), replace = TRUE), ]
  coef(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = boot_sample))["wt"]
})

boot_df <- data.frame(slope = boot_coefs)
```


Exercise 3.1 - Before plotting, compute mean(boot_df$slope) and sd(boot_df$slope), and compare to the SE reported by summary(fit2). Are they similar? What would you expect, and why?


```{r}
summary(fit2)

mean(boot_df$slope) 
sd(boot_df$slope)
```
They are similar enough. This is what I would expect, given enough bootstrapping rounds i would expect the mean and sd for the slope to settle around the actual values because the bootstrapping is pulling random smaples from the data. Given enough samples the mean of their means will tend to the population mean. Achieved through simulation. This is the plug-in principle. By re sampling the sample, we are treating the sample like a population. And so the bootstrap sample will eventually approximate the sample. 

#Visualising the bootstrap distribution
##Density and violin

```{r}
ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(fit2)["wt"], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap distribution of the slope (mpg ~ wt)",
       x = "Slope estimate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = "wt", y = slope)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap distribution (violin + jitter)",
       x = NULL, y = "Slope estimate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

##Quantile dotplot

```{r}
# A simple quantile dotplot: discretise into 50 equally-likely outcomes
n_dots <- 50
q_vals <- quantile(boot_df$slope, probs = seq(0.5/n_dots, 1 - 0.5/n_dots, length.out = n_dots))
dot_df <- data.frame(slope = q_vals)

ggplot(dot_df, aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = diff(range(q_vals))/30, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Quantile dotplot (50 dots)",
       x = "Slope estimate", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Exercise 3.2 - Build a 1x3 comparison figure: (a) point + 95% CI error bar, (b) density/violin, (c) quantile dotplot, all showing the same bootstrap distribution of the slope. For each, write one sentence describing what additional information it conveys relative to (a).

```{r, warning=FALSE}
original_slope <- coef(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))["wt"]

plot_data <- data.frame(
  term = "wt",
  estimate = original_slope,
  conf.low = ci_95[1], 
  conf.high = ci_95[2] 
)

A <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = term, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 1) +         
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  coord_flip() +                      
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap 95% Confidence Interval for Slope (wt)",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Slope Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

B <- ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(fit2)["wt"], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap distribution of the slope (mpg ~ wt)",
       x = "Slope estimate") +
  theme_minimal()

C <- ggplot(dot_df, aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = diff(range(q_vals))/30, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Quantile dotplot (50 dots)",
       x = "Slope estimate", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=5}
A | B | C
```

forest plot shows the estaimte of the slope from the bootstrapping with 95% confidence interval. It says the real slope is probalby in here, at the dot and between the lines. 
The density plot shows how the model estimates of the slope are distributed. It shows that the mena was around -5.4 or so with most estiamtes between -6 and -5. Not showing the confidence internal. 
The quantile dotplot shows that each dot is equally likely, and the stack with the most dots/highest stack is the most likely one. From the bootstrapping. just under -5. This was the most frequently estimated value. Similar to density, but discrete not continuous.
